=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter
Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of
Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and
look forward to your mark-up.
SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)
Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims
is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.
Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and
only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the
basket is recoverable.
Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after
Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims
unless expressly stated otherwise.
Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same
caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.
Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and
non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.
Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public
registers (see Disclosure Letter).
Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the
Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or
public records.
Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller
will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the
counterparty's written consent.
Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding)
will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.
Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing
bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds
flow.)
Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio
matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.
Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter
and is not expected to be material.
Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course
operating costs.
Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime
above.
Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.
Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and
records are fictional.
1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the
indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including
DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly
searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific
disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent,
payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.
2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause
11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final
written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.
3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2.
As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security
is included.
4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of
every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of
non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.
5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject
to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft
Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or
on-costs apply.
6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external
email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity
timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised
person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation
remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no
loss amount.

a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.
8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each
(AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether
each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

consent is required merely because shares are sold.

the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the
Buyer has completed its own verification.

must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer assessment

**Do not accept this package as drafted.** Its central problem is the combination of broad disclosure and deemed buyer knowledge with limitations applying to **all Claims**. That could leave Wattlebridge bearing known problems while also losing meaningful remedies for unknown ones.

This review is based on the Seller’s summaries and Disclosure Letter—not the underlying SPA or DD documents. The facts disclosed identify risks; they do not establish that every consent is required, liability has arisen or amount should be deducted from the price.

## 1. Preserve meaningful remedies

### Blanket application of limitations — priority pushback

Clauses 12.3/13 and 9.3/12.8/20.5 potentially extend the general warranty cap, thresholds, time limits, exclusive-remedy provisions and non-reliance provisions to every claim.

**Why this matters:** Even a separately negotiated indemnity or completion obligation could become subject to the AUD 4.8 million cap, AUD 250,000 deductible and 18-month deadline. Calling something an “indemnity” does not protect it if the general limitations override it.

**Push back:**
- Establish separate, expressly identified regimes for general warranties, fundamental/title warranties, tax, specific indemnities and contractual obligations.
- Exclude purchase-price adjustments, debt repayment, completion deliverables and other payment obligations from general warranty limitations.
- Preserve appropriate termination, enforcement and equitable remedies.
- Carve out Seller fraud and fraudulent concealment; preserve rights that cannot lawfully be excluded. Review any broader misconduct carve-outs expressly.
- Make the drafting hierarchy clear: specific protections must prevail over general limitations.

### General warranty cap, thresholds and time limits

The Seller proposes:
- **20% cap:** AUD 4.8 million;
- **AUD 25,000 de minimis:** a claim must exceed it;
- **AUD 250,000 deductible basket:** only the excess is recoverable;
- **18-month notification period.**

These are negotiating positions, not inherently acceptable terms. Their combined effect could leave substantial losses with the Buyer.

**Push back:**
- Seek a higher cap, informed by DD, available recovery security and any warranty insurance.
- Reduce thresholds and seek a **tipping basket**, under which qualifying losses are recoverable from the first dollar once the basket is exceeded.
- Aggregate related claims for threshold purposes to prevent fragmentation.
- Seek at least 24 months for general warranties, allowing sufficient post-completion reporting cycles.
- Ensure timely notified claims survive until resolved. Reject overly technical notice requirements or an unduly short deadline to commence proceedings.

The general regime should not govern the separate categories below.

### Fundamental/title, tax and IP protection

**Fundamental/title:** Reject the proposal to treat these like general warranties “for administrative simplicity”. Ownership and capacity are central to buying 100% of the company. Seek a purchase-price-level cap or uncapped protection as appropriate, no de minimis or basket, and materially longer survival aligned with applicable limitation periods.

**Tax:** Do not regard this as settled. Require an effective pre-completion tax indemnity, suitable tax warranties, a separate cap and survival through relevant assessment/reassessment periods plus a claim-notification buffer. Address transaction-related taxes and allocation consistently with the agreed economics.

**IP:** For an analytics business, ownership and rights to use core IP may be value-critical. Assess broader IP warranty protection separately from the general package. Ironquay needs its own solution.

## 2. Reject disclosure and knowledge provisions that transfer DD risk to the Buyer

The Seller seeks to disclose the entire data room, documents merely “referred to”, accounts, registers and public records. Clause 8.3 goes further: it treats matters **discoverable** by the Buyer or advisers as known.

**Why this matters:** The Seller could argue that an obscure reference, incomplete document or uninvestigated risk defeats a warranty claim. A disclosure of uncertainty is not the same as clear disclosure of the nature and scope of a warranty exception.

**Push back:**
- Require **fair disclosure with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter**, preferably against identified warranties.
- Reject blanket incorporation of the data room and public records. Any agreed general disclosures should be tightly specified.
- Freeze and retain the agreed disclosure bundle and index; prevent unilateral late updates from qualifying signing or completion warranties.
- Delete constructive/deemed knowledge and adviser-knowledge attribution. Prefer no knowledge exclusion; if conceded, confine it to actual knowledge of named Buyer deal principals, without a duty to investigate.
- State expressly that disclosure and Buyer knowledge do **not** qualify specific indemnities or excuse compliance with completion obligations.

The Seller’s reservation that the letter admits no liability does not itself resolve any issue. Equally, the Buyer should not assume that disclosure creates a remedy.

## 3. Deal-specific risks requiring action

| Issue | Buyer concern and recommended response |
|---|---|
| **Bluefen — approximately AUD 3.6 million / 30% of FY26 revenue** | A material customer dependency. The Disclosure Letter expressly says no final written consent or evidence of satisfaction of associated conditions is included. **Reasonable endeavours is not a substitute for achieving the required outcome.** Require a Buyer-waivable condition precedent for valid consent satisfying clauses 11.2–11.3, with no unacceptable conditions or adverse contract changes. Review the actual consent and associated requirements. Include a long-stop date and appropriate termination rights. Do not deem the condition satisfied merely on delivery of a document labelled “consent”. |
| **Riverlark — approximately AUD 3.2 million debt** | A release **after** Completion is inconsistent with delivering an effectively debt-free business and leaves security and change-of-control exposure with the Buyer. Require a verified payoff amount, payment through the completion funds flow, and effective discharge/release arrangements contemporaneous with Completion. Any later administrative register removal should be backed by binding release evidence and prompt filing obligations. Reflect the debt in the agreed price mechanics **without double counting** its deduction and repayment. |
| **Ironquay IP — AUD 180,000 recorded open** | The disclosed clause makes transfer of SOW3 materials conditional on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. The ledger is not conclusive proof of non-payment, but the evidence does not establish transfer either. Verify all relevant fees and obtain payment evidence, an effective confirmatory assignment and appropriate releases by Completion. Check the wider chain of title. A payment-only indemnity is inadequate if the real loss is inability to own or use important IP: seek protection covering resulting ownership/use claims and remediation costs, outside general warranty restrictions. |
| **Completion bonuses — AUD 420,000 plus possible on-costs** | Their omission from the funds flow is a material economic gap. Saying they are “a matter for the Seller” does not prevent a Company liability from passing economically to the Buyer. Confirm recipients, conditions, employing entity, payment timing, withholding and applicable superannuation/payroll-tax/on-cost treatment. Negotiate Seller funding or a corresponding price adjustment for these transaction-triggered bonuses and associated costs; itemise the agreed treatment and avoid double counting. Separately distinguish any genuinely Buyer-agreed post-completion retention arrangements. |
| **Export/privacy incident — potentially 1,240 records** | The evidence does **not** establish unauthorised access, a notifiable breach or a loss amount. But “preliminary” does not establish immateriality. Require investigation updates and evidence concerning access, containment, scope, applicable privacy/customer obligations and notification requirements. Require timely lawful remediation and preservation of evidence. Seek a specific indemnity for the pre-completion incident and resulting lawful liabilities and reasonable investigation/remediation costs, unaffected by disclosure or knowledge. Consider a completion condition or retention if the investigation reveals material unresolved exposure. |
| **Sandbar renewals — AUD 330,000 aggregate** | Neither “ordinary course” nor debt-like treatment is established. Review DD-008 and DD-011 together for execution dates, service periods, termination rights, accruals and necessity. Treat related renewals together under pre-completion covenant/consent thresholds. Costs properly attributable to ongoing post-completion services may be operating costs; pre-completion accruals, unusual commitments or leakage may require different treatment under the price mechanics. Do not automatically deduct all AUD 330,000. |
| **Title — DD-012 share register** | The register is relevant evidence, not a complete title investigation. Verify the capital structure, issue and transfer history, options/convertibles, encumbrances, pre-emption rights and any competing beneficial interests. Require effective transfer documents, corporate approvals, release of share security where relevant and robust title warranties at Completion. |

## 4. Avoid demanding consents the documents do not support

Two points need disciplined treatment:

- **Office lease:** The disclosure identifies a **notification** obligation, not landlord consent to the share sale. Review the lease and require timely compliant notification and evidence of delivery; do not assume a consent condition.
- **Mossvale:** An assignment restriction does not automatically apply to a share sale. Check for a separate change-of-control provision, deemed-assignment wording or transaction step involving assignment. Require consent only if the actual terms and structure warrant it.

These distinctions keep negotiations focused on genuine execution risks.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Fix the liability architecture:** separate general warranties from title, tax, specific indemnities and completion/payment obligations.
2. **Protect completion:** substantive Bluefen consent; Riverlark payoff and effective releases at Completion; verified title and Ironquay IP ownership.
3. **Close the economic gaps:** expressly allocate bonuses and on-costs; reconcile debt and renewal treatment without double counting.
4. **Preserve recourse:** narrow disclosure, remove deemed knowledge, and strengthen the general cap, basket and survival period.
5. **Resolve uncertainty with evidence and security:** complete the incident investigation and consider targeted retention/escrow for unresolved exposures, supported by effective indemnities.

**Bottom line:** Do not accept known risks merely because they are disclosed. Each material issue needs a verified resolution, an express economic allocation, or an enforceable remedy backed by a credible recovery source.
